When I rated this movie five stars last year, I think I was wearing rose-colored glasses during the second half because I wanted any excuse to show all of my love towards the first half. Now, the first half is one of the finest hours of any movies I've ever seen, and the title drop gives me goosebumps. However, the second half loses the pessimistic tone from the first half and adopts this macho war-film tone. I wouldn't be surprised if they played Fortunate Son during it because it felt that cliche. Joker literally tells the audience the theme of the movie which is like a crime for a Kubrick movie. In my opinion, Kubrick's best aspect is how vague his movies are and how they are interpreted. This movie does not leave room for interpretation. This movie is amazingly directed and the ending is spectacular. However, now that I've watched more movies and more Kubricks, this movie feels a lot less cinematic and breathtaking than it first did. However, the first half is five stars and one of the greatest hours of film to ever be recorded and that's why I still love it.

The full metal jacket is the hard casing around the bullet. Kubrick spends the first half of the film showing us how a similar shell can be built around men. In the back half, he shows us the result of that transformation. Like Joker, we're left confused and numb by the traumatic end to the first act, the change of pace, and the lack of a clear objective as we witness the vulgar humor, dehumanization of the enemy & self, and desensitization to horror that allow people to become cruel enough to survive in “a world of shit”. Full Metal Jacket is another Kubrick movie where I think the reputation is completely justified. It’s brutal, darkly funny, emotionally cold, and remarkably controlled. If A Clockwork Orange asks whether the state can take away someone’s free will in the name of creating a better person, Full Metal Jacket asks a related question: What happens when an institution deliberately destroys your humanity because it believes that will make you better at killing? Kubrick’s answer is basically: you may become very good at killing but something inside you has already died.
